notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Biological evolution is the gradual change in inherited characteristics of populations over successive generations.
  • Evolution occurs in populations, not because an individual organism deliberately changes itself.
  • Genetic variation provides the raw material for evolution.
  • Important evolutionary mechanisms include natural selection, mutation, genetic drift, gene flow and recombination.
  • Evolution explains both the diversity and common ancestry of living organisms.
  • Evolution does not necessarily mean progress toward greater complexity.
  • Natural selection is one major mechanism of evolution, but it is not the only mechanism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Evolution → Heritable Change in Populations Across Generations

2. Origin of Life vs Evolution
  • Origin of life deals with how the first living systems arose from non-living matter.
  • Biological evolution deals with changes occurring after life already existed.
  • These are related but distinct scientific questions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Origin of life ≠ Biological evolution.

3. Age of Earth
  • Earth is approximately 4.54 billion years old.
  • The earliest evidence for life dates back more than 3 billion years.
  • Early Earth had very different atmospheric and environmental conditions from the present.
4. Early Ideas About Origin of Life

Historical ideas included:

  • Special creation.
  • Spontaneous generation.
  • Biogenesis.
  • Chemical evolution.
  • Modern biology rejects spontaneous generation under present ordinary conditions.
5. Spontaneous Generation
  • Spontaneous generation was the old belief that living organisms could arise directly from non-living matter under ordinary conditions.
  • Examples once believed included maggots arising from meat.
  • Experiments by Redi, Spallanzani and Pasteur helped disprove this idea.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spontaneous Generation → Disproved Experimentally

6. Francesco Redi
  • Francesco Redi performed experiments using meat in jars.
  • Maggots appeared only when flies could reach the meat.
  • His work challenged spontaneous generation.
  • His famous experiments were conducted in the seventeenth century.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Redi → Meat + Maggots Experiment

7. Lazzaro Spallanzani
  • Spallanzani boiled nutrient broths and sealed them.
  • Sealed broths remained free from microbial growth.
  • His experiments provided evidence against spontaneous generation.
8. Louis Pasteur
  • Louis Pasteur conclusively challenged spontaneous generation using swan-neck flask experiments.
  • Broth remained sterile while airborne microorganisms were prevented from reaching it.
  • When contamination occurred, microorganisms grew.
  • Pasteur's work strongly supported biogenesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pasteur → Swan-Neck Flask → Biogenesis

9. Biogenesis
  • Biogenesis means life arises from pre-existing life under present biological conditions.
  • Virchow's idea that cells arise from pre-existing cells is consistent with biogenesis.
  • Biogenesis does not explain how the first life originated.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Biogenesis explains present reproduction of life, not the initial origin of life.

10. Chemical Evolution
  • Chemical evolution proposes that the first living systems arose gradually from non-living chemical substances on early Earth.
  • Simple inorganic substances could have formed increasingly complex organic molecules.
  • These could eventually have contributed to self-replicating systems.
11. Oparin and Haldane
  • Alexander Oparin and J. B. S. Haldane independently proposed ideas of chemical evolution.
  • They suggested that organic molecules could form under primitive Earth conditions.
  • Their ideas are often called the Oparin-Haldane hypothesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Oparin + Haldane → Chemical Evolution

12. Primordial Soup
  • The phrase primordial soup refers to the idea of an early environment containing accumulated organic molecules.
  • Such molecules could have participated in further chemical evolution.
  • This is a conceptual model rather than a literal uniform ocean of organic material.
13. Miller-Urey Experiment
  • Stanley Miller and Harold Urey performed a famous experiment in 1953.
  • They simulated certain hypothesised early-Earth atmospheric conditions.
  • Electrical sparks represented lightning.
  • Organic molecules, including amino acids, were produced.
📌 Must-Memorise

Miller-Urey Experiment → 1953 → Amino Acids

14. Significance of Miller-Urey Experiment
  • The experiment showed that organic molecules can form abiotically under some plausible prebiotic conditions.
  • It did not create life.
  • It did not prove the exact composition of early Earth's atmosphere.
  • It provided experimental support for chemical evolution.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Miller-Urey → Produced organic molecules, not living organisms.

15. First Genetic Material — RNA World Idea
  • The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA may have preceded modern DNA-protein systems.
  • RNA can store information.
  • Some RNA molecules can catalyse reactions.
  • Catalytic RNA molecules are called ribozymes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RNA World → RNA as Information + Catalyst

16. Protocells
  • Protocells are simple membrane-like structures proposed as steps toward early cellular life.
  • Lipid molecules can spontaneously form vesicles in water.
  • Compartmentalisation could have helped concentrate reacting molecules.
17. Earliest Life Forms
  • The earliest life forms were probably simple and microscopic.
  • They were prokaryote-like.
  • Early life existed before oxygen became abundant in Earth's atmosphere.
  • Anaerobic metabolism likely preceded widespread aerobic respiration.
18. Photosynthesis and Atmospheric Oxygen
  • Early photosynthetic microorganisms gradually changed Earth's atmosphere.
  • Cyanobacteria played a major role in oxygenic photosynthesis.
  • Oxygen accumulation eventually enabled widespread aerobic metabolism.
  • Increased oxygen also allowed formation of the stratospheric ozone layer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cyanobacteria → Major Early Oxygen Producers

19. Great Oxidation Event
  • Atmospheric oxygen rose significantly roughly 2.4 billion years ago.
  • This major environmental transition is called the Great Oxidation Event.
  • It transformed Earth's chemistry and biological evolution.
20. Evolutionary Thought Before Darwin

Important historical figures include:

  • Buffon.
  • Erasmus Darwin.
  • Lamarck.
  • Charles Darwin.
  • Alfred Russel Wallace.
21. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
  • Lamarck proposed an early scientific theory of evolution.
  • His major evolutionary work Philosophie Zoologique was published in 1809.
  • He believed organisms changed through use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lamarck → Inheritance of Acquired Characters → 1809

22. Lamarckism

Major ideas included:

  • Changing environment creates new needs.
  • Organs used frequently become stronger.
  • Organs not used become reduced.
  • Acquired characteristics were proposed to be inherited.
📌 Classic Example

Giraffes were proposed to have developed long necks through repeated stretching over generations.

23. Use and Disuse
  • Lamarck suggested that frequent use strengthens organs.
  • Lack of use causes organs to degenerate.
  • This was one component of Lamarck's theory.
24. Inheritance of Acquired Characters
  • Lamarck proposed that traits acquired during an individual's lifetime could be passed to offspring.
  • Classical genetics does not support this as a general mechanism of evolution.
  • Modern epigenetics does not restore Lamarck's original theory as a general explanation of evolution.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lamarckism ≠ Modern evolutionary theory.

25. August Weismann
  • August Weismann argued against inheritance of acquired somatic characteristics.
  • He distinguished germ cells from body cells.
  • His germ-plasm theory influenced modern heredity concepts.
  • His mouse-tail experiment is frequently cited in school-level discussions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Weismann → Germ-Plasm Theory

26. Charles Darwin
  • Charles Darwin developed the theory of evolution by natural selection.
  • He was born in 1809.
  • He travelled aboard HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836.
  • Observations during the voyage strongly influenced his evolutionary ideas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darwin → Natural Selection

27. HMS Beagle
  • Darwin served as a naturalist during the voyage of HMS Beagle.
  • The voyage lasted roughly five years.
  • He studied geology, fossils, plants and animals.
  • The Galápagos Islands became especially important in later discussions of his observations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darwin → HMS Beagle

28. Galápagos Islands
  • The Galápagos Islands are located in the Pacific Ocean near Ecuador.
  • Darwin observed related organisms differing among islands.
  • Finches and tortoises became famous examples in evolutionary discussions.
  • The pattern suggested adaptation and common ancestry.
29. Darwin's Finches
  • Galápagos finches show variation in beak form.
  • Different beak shapes are associated with different feeding niches.
  • They became a classic example of adaptive radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darwin's Finches → Adaptive Radiation

30. Alfred Russel Wallace
  • Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea of natural selection.
  • His work prompted joint presentation of Darwin and Wallace's ideas in 1858.
  • Wallace conducted important studies in Southeast Asia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darwin + Wallace → Natural Selection

31. Darwin-Wallace Joint Presentation
  • Darwin and Wallace's papers on natural selection were presented jointly to the Linnean Society of London in 1858.
  • This preceded Darwin's major book.
32. On the Origin of Species
  • Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
  • The book explained evolution primarily through natural selection.
  • It presented extensive evidence for common descent and modification over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Darwin → Origin of Species → 1859

33. Natural Selection
  • Natural selection occurs when individuals differ in inherited traits affecting survival or reproduction.
  • Individuals with advantageous heritable traits leave more offspring on average.
  • Those traits become more common over generations.
  • Natural selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies in populations.
34. Main Conditions for Natural Selection

Natural selection requires:

  • Variation among individuals.
  • Heritability of at least some variation.
  • Differences in survival or reproduction.
  • More offspring than can all survive under limited resources.
35. Overproduction
  • Organisms often produce more offspring than can survive to reproduce.
  • Resources are limited.
  • This creates competition and differential survival.
36. Struggle for Existence

Darwin described competition broadly as struggle for existence.

It may involve:

  • Competition for food.
  • Competition for space.
  • Predation.
  • Disease.
  • Environmental stress.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

“Struggle” does not mean only direct physical fighting.

37. Survival of the Fittest
  • Herbert Spencer coined the phrase survival of the fittest.
  • Darwin later used the phrase.
  • Fitness in evolution means reproductive success, not simply physical strength.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Herbert Spencer → “Survival of the Fittest”

38. Biological Fitness
  • Fitness is an organism's relative contribution of offspring to future generations.
  • Higher fitness means greater reproductive success in a particular environment.
  • A trait advantageous in one environment may be disadvantageous in another.
39. Adaptation Through Natural Selection
  • Natural selection increases the frequency of traits that improve reproductive success.
  • Adaptations arise across generations.
  • Organisms do not consciously evolve traits because they “need” them.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Need does not directly create evolutionary traits.

40. Variation
  • Variation refers to differences among individuals.
  • Variations can result from genetic and environmental causes.
  • Heritable genetic variation is particularly important for evolution.
41. Sources of Genetic Variation

Major sources include:

  • Mutation.
  • Crossing over.
  • Independent assortment.
  • Random fertilisation.
  • Gene flow.
42. Mutation
  • Mutation is a change in genetic material.
  • Mutations create new alleles.
  • Mutations occur randomly with respect to an organism's needs.
  • Mutations may be beneficial, harmful or neutral.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mutation → Source of New Genetic Variation

43. Hugo de Vries
  • Hugo de Vries proposed mutation theory in the early twentieth century.
  • He studied evening primrose, Oenothera.
  • He emphasised mutations as sources of evolutionary change.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hugo de Vries → Mutation Theory

44. Recombination
  • Sexual reproduction reshuffles existing genetic variation.
  • Crossing over occurs during meiosis.
  • Independent assortment produces different chromosome combinations.
  • Recombination creates new allele combinations.
45. Gene Flow
  • Gene flow is movement of alleles between populations.
  • Migration followed by reproduction produces gene flow.
  • Gene flow can reduce genetic differences between populations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gene Flow → Allele Movement Between Populations

46. Genetic Drift
  • Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies.
  • Its effects are strongest in small populations.
  • Drift can cause alleles to become fixed or lost regardless of selective advantage.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Genetic Drift → Random Allele-Frequency Change

47. Founder Effect
  • Founder effect occurs when a new population is established by a small number of individuals.
  • The new population may have allele frequencies very different from the original population.
  • It is a form of genetic drift.
48. Bottleneck Effect
  • Population bottleneck occurs when population size is drastically reduced.
  • The surviving population may contain only a fraction of original genetic diversity.
  • Subsequent generations can show altered allele frequencies.
  • It is a form of genetic drift.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Founder Effect + Bottleneck → Genetic Drift

49. Natural Selection vs Genetic Drift
  • Natural selection is non-random with respect to fitness.
  • Genetic drift changes allele frequencies randomly.
  • Both can alter populations over generations.
50. Directional Selection
  • Directional selection favours one extreme phenotype.
  • Population average shifts toward that extreme.
  • Antibiotic resistance under drug exposure can involve directional selection.
51. Stabilising Selection
  • Stabilising selection favours intermediate phenotypes.
  • Extreme forms are selected against.
  • Variation around the mean decreases.
  • Human birth weight is often used as a classic example.
52. Disruptive Selection
  • Disruptive selection favours both extremes over intermediate forms.
  • It can increase variation within a population.
  • Under some conditions, it may contribute to divergence.
53. Artificial Selection
  • Artificial selection is selective breeding controlled by humans.
  • Humans choose organisms with desirable traits to reproduce.
  • Domestic dog breeds and crop varieties are examples.
  • Darwin used artificial selection as an analogy for natural selection.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Artificial Selection → Human-Directed Selection

54. Domestication
  • Domestication changes wild species through human selection.
  • Dogs evolved from wolf ancestors through long-term domestication and selection.
  • Crops such as maize have been transformed from wild ancestors.
55. Antibiotic Resistance
  • Antibiotics do not deliberately create resistant bacteria.
  • Resistant variants may already exist or arise by mutation.
  • Antibiotic treatment kills susceptible bacteria.
  • Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.
  • Misuse and overuse accelerate selection for resistance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Antibiotic resistance → Natural selection, not “bacteria deciding to adapt.”

56. Pesticide Resistance
  • Repeated use of the same pesticide selects resistant pests.
  • Resistant individuals survive.
  • They reproduce and increase resistance frequency.
  • This is another clear example of evolution by natural selection.
57. Industrial Melanism
  • Industrial melanism refers to increased frequency of dark-coloured forms in polluted industrial environments.
  • Peppered moths in Britain are the classic example.
  • Dark moths had better camouflage on soot-darkened surfaces in polluted areas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peppered Moth → Industrial Melanism

58. Peppered Moth
  • Biston betularia is the peppered moth.
  • Before heavy industrial pollution, light-coloured forms were common in many areas.
  • Soot darkened tree surfaces and reduced lichens.
  • Dark forms gained a camouflage advantage in polluted habitats.
  • Pollution controls later altered these selective conditions.
59. Adaptation Examples

Examples include:

  • Camouflage.
  • Mimicry.
  • Thick fur in cold climates.
  • Cactus water-storage adaptations.
  • Bird beak diversity.
  • Antibiotic resistance.
60. Camouflage
  • Camouflage reduces detection by blending with surroundings.
  • It can help predators approach prey.
  • It can help prey avoid predators.
  • Natural selection can shape camouflage patterns.
61. Mimicry
  • Mimicry occurs when one organism resembles another organism or object.
  • It can reduce predation or provide another selective advantage.
62. Batesian Mimicry
  • In Batesian mimicry, a harmless or palatable species resembles a harmful or unpalatable species.
  • Predators may avoid the mimic because of its resemblance to the model.
63. Müllerian Mimicry
  • In Müllerian mimicry, two or more genuinely harmful or unpalatable species share similar warning signals.
  • Predators learn avoidance more efficiently.
64. Evidence for Evolution

Major evidence comes from:

  • Fossils.
  • Comparative anatomy.
  • Embryology.
  • Vestigial organs.
  • Biogeography.
  • Molecular biology.
  • Genetics.
  • Direct observation of evolutionary change.
65. Fossils
  • Fossils are preserved remains, impressions or traces of past organisms.
  • They occur mainly in sedimentary rocks.
  • Fossils provide direct historical evidence of past life.
  • Fossil succession helps reconstruct evolutionary history.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fossils → Evidence of Past Life

66. Palaeontology
  • Palaeontology is the scientific study of fossils and ancient life.
  • Fossil evidence helps reconstruct extinct organisms and evolutionary transitions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Palaeontology → Fossils

67. Fossilisation

Fossilisation can occur through:

  • Mineral replacement.
  • Impressions.
  • Moulds and casts.
  • Amber preservation.
  • Freezing.
  • Carbonisation.
  • Fossilisation is rare because most organisms decompose completely.
68. Relative Dating
  • Relative dating determines whether one fossil or rock layer is older or younger than another.
  • Deeper undisturbed sedimentary layers are generally older than layers above them.
  • This principle is associated with stratigraphy.
69. Absolute Dating
  • Absolute dating estimates numerical ages.
  • Radioactive isotopes are used.
  • Carbon-14 is useful for relatively recent organic remains.
  • Potassium-argon and uranium-lead methods are useful for much older rocks.
70. Archaeopteryx
  • Archaeopteryx is an important fossil showing a combination of dinosaur/reptile-like and bird-like features.
  • It possessed feathers and wings.
  • It also had teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail.
  • It lived during the Late Jurassic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Archaeopteryx → Transitional Fossil Between Non-Avian Dinosaurs and Birds

71. Connecting Link
  • A connecting link is an organism showing features of two different groups in traditional textbook terminology.
  • Archaeopteryx is often cited between reptiles/dinosaurs and birds.
  • Peripatus is traditionally cited between annelids and arthropods.
  • Lungfish are sometimes cited for fish–tetrapod-related features in older texts.
📌 TNPSC Note

“Connecting link” is a traditional exam term; modern evolutionary biology describes lineages and shared ancestry more precisely.

72. Peripatus
  • Peripatus belongs to phylum Onychophora.
  • It possesses features historically compared with annelids and arthropods.
  • It is often called a connecting link in textbook classification questions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peripatus → Annelid–Arthropod Connecting-Link Example

73. Comparative Anatomy
  • Comparative anatomy compares structures in different organisms.
  • Similar structures may indicate common ancestry.
  • Homologous and analogous organs are important concepts.
74. Homologous Organs
  • Homologous organs have the same basic structural origin but may perform different functions.
  • They indicate common ancestry and divergent evolution.
  • Forelimbs of humans, whales, bats and horses are classic examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homologous → Same Basic Origin, Different Functions

75. Pentadactyl Limb
  • Many tetrapods share a five-digit basic limb pattern.
  • Human arm, bat wing, whale flipper and horse forelimb are modifications of a common structural plan.
  • This is strong evidence of common ancestry.
76. Divergent Evolution
  • Divergent evolution occurs when related organisms become increasingly different.
  • Homologous structures are associated with divergent evolution.
  • Different environments can favour different adaptations from a common ancestral structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Homologous Organs → Divergent Evolution

77. Analogous Organs
  • Analogous organs perform similar functions but have different evolutionary origins and structures.
  • Wings of birds and insects are common textbook examples.
  • Analogous structures result from convergent evolution.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Analogous → Same Function, Different Origin

78. Convergent Evolution
  • Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated lineages independently evolve similar adaptations.
  • Similar environmental pressures can produce similar functional solutions.
  • Bird wings and insect wings are an example at a broad functional level.
  • Streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins are another example.
📌 Must-Memorise

Analogous Organs → Convergent Evolution

79. Vestigial Organs
  • Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of features that had larger or different functions in ancestors.
  • They provide evidence of evolutionary history.
  • Vestigial does not always mean completely functionless.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vestigial ≠ Necessarily useless.

80. Human Vestigial Structures

Common textbook examples include:

  • Coccyx.
  • Appendix.
  • Wisdom teeth.
  • Ear-moving muscles.
  • Small body-hair muscles.
  • Several retain minor functions but are reduced relative to ancestral forms.
81. Embryological Evidence
  • Related organisms can show similar developmental patterns.
  • Vertebrate embryos share several early structural features.
  • Developmental similarities can reflect common ancestry.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

The old claim that “ontogeny exactly recapitulates phylogeny” is not accepted in its strict form.

82. Ernst Haeckel
  • Ernst Haeckel promoted the recapitulation idea.
  • He coined the phrase “ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny.”
  • Modern embryology does not accept this as a literal law.
83. Biogeography
  • Biogeography studies geographic distribution of organisms.
  • Island species often resemble nearby mainland relatives while showing unique adaptations.
  • Geographic isolation can promote speciation.
84. Wallace Line
  • Wallace Line is a biogeographic boundary in Southeast Asia.
  • It separates faunal regions with strongly different evolutionary histories.
  • It is named after Alfred Russel Wallace.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wallace → Wallace Line + Natural Selection

85. Molecular Evidence
  • DNA and protein sequence similarities reveal evolutionary relationships.
  • Closely related organisms generally have more similar DNA sequences.
  • Universal genetic code and shared biochemical pathways support common ancestry.
86. Cytochrome c Evidence
  • Cytochrome c is a conserved protein involved in cellular respiration.
  • Sequence differences among species can be used to infer evolutionary relationships.
  • Fewer differences generally indicate closer evolutionary relationship.
87. DNA Evidence
  • DNA comparison provides powerful evidence of common ancestry.
  • Mutations accumulate over time.
  • Shared unusual mutations can indicate shared ancestry.
  • Molecular phylogenies help reconstruct evolutionary trees.
88. Common Genetic Code
  • Nearly all organisms use essentially the same genetic code.
  • This universality supports common ancestry of life.
  • A few minor variations occur in mitochondria and some microorganisms.
89. Speciation
  • Speciation is formation of new species.
  • It requires populations to diverge genetically.
  • Reproductive isolation is central to many forms of speciation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Speciation → Formation of New Species

90. Reproductive Isolation
  • Reproductive isolation prevents gene flow between populations.
  • It may occur before fertilisation or after fertilisation.
  • Over time, isolated populations can evolve independently.
91. Prezygotic Isolation

Examples include:

  • Geographic isolation.
  • Habitat isolation.
  • Temporal isolation.
  • Behavioural isolation.
  • Mechanical isolation.
  • Gametic isolation.
  • These prevent mating or fertilisation.
92. Postzygotic Isolation
  • Postzygotic barriers act after fertilisation.
  • Hybrid offspring may have reduced viability.
  • Hybrids may be sterile.
  • Mule sterility is a familiar example.
93. Allopatric Speciation
  • Allopatric speciation occurs when populations become geographically separated.
  • Mountains, rivers, islands or distance can prevent gene flow.
  • Independent evolution can lead to reproductive isolation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Allopatric → Geographic Isolation

94. Sympatric Speciation
  • Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic separation.
  • Polyploidy is an important mechanism in plants.
  • Ecological and reproductive differences can also contribute.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sympatric → Same Geographic Area

95. Polyploidy
  • Polyploid organisms possess more than two complete chromosome sets.
  • Polyploidy is common in plants.
  • It can produce rapid reproductive isolation.
  • Many crop plants are polyploid.
96. Adaptive Radiation
  • Adaptive radiation is rapid diversification of one ancestral lineage into multiple forms adapted to different ecological niches.
  • Darwin's finches are a classic example.
  • Australian marsupials provide another classic textbook example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Adaptive Radiation → One Ancestor → Many Ecological Forms

97. Extinction
  • Extinction is permanent disappearance of a species.
  • Most species that have ever lived are extinct.
  • Extinction may result from environmental change, competition, disease, catastrophes or human activity.
98. Mass Extinction
  • Mass extinctions involve unusually rapid loss of large numbers of species globally.
  • Earth's history includes five major recognised mass-extinction events.
  • The end-Permian extinction was the largest known.
  • The end-Cretaceous extinction eliminated non-avian dinosaurs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Mass Extinction → End-Permian

99. Dinosaur Extinction
  • Non-avian dinosaurs disappeared about 66 million years ago.
  • A large asteroid impact near present-day Chicxulub, Mexico, was a major cause.
  • Massive environmental changes followed.
  • Birds are surviving descendants of theropod dinosaurs.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Birds are evolutionarily within the dinosaur lineage.

100. Natural Selection and Extinction
  • Natural selection cannot guarantee survival of a species.
  • Rapid environmental change can exceed a population's capacity to adapt.
  • Small populations may be especially vulnerable.
101. Hardy-Weinberg Principle
  • Hardy-Weinberg principle describes allele frequencies in an ideal non-evolving population.
  • It provides a null model for population genetics.
  • If assumptions are met, allele frequencies remain constant across generations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hardy-Weinberg → Genetic Equilibrium

102. Hardy-Weinberg Equation

For two alleles:

p + q = 1

p² + 2pq + q² = 1

Where:

  • p and q are allele frequencies.
  • p² and q² are homozygote frequencies.
  • 2pq is heterozygote frequency.
📌 Must-Memorise

p² + 2pq + q² = 1

103. Hardy-Weinberg Conditions

Ideal conditions include:

  • Very large population.
  • Random mating.
  • No mutation.
  • No migration/gene flow.
  • No natural selection.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Violation of Hardy-Weinberg Conditions → Evolutionary Change Possible

104. Causes of Change from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
  • Mutation.
  • Natural selection.
  • Gene flow.
  • Genetic drift.
  • Non-random mating can change genotype frequencies.
105. Microevolution
  • Microevolution refers to changes in allele frequencies within populations.
  • Natural selection and genetic drift produce microevolution.
  • Antibiotic resistance is an observable example.
106. Macroevolution
  • Macroevolution refers to large-scale evolutionary patterns over long periods.
  • It includes speciation, extinction and diversification of major lineages.
  • Macroevolution builds on population-level evolutionary processes.
107. Gradualism
  • Gradualism proposes that evolutionary change can accumulate through many small changes over long periods.
  • Darwin broadly emphasised gradual evolutionary change.
108. Punctuated Equilibrium
  • Punctuated equilibrium proposes long periods of relative evolutionary stability interrupted by comparatively rapid evolutionary change associated with speciation.
  • Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge proposed this model in 1972.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gould + Eldredge → Punctuated Equilibrium

109. Human Evolution — Basic Facts
  • Humans are primates.
  • Modern humans belong to species Homo sapiens.
  • Humans did not evolve from modern chimpanzees.
  • Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor.
  • Human evolution involved branching lineages, not a simple straight ladder.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Humans did not evolve from present-day monkeys or chimpanzees.

110. Human Taxonomic Position

Humans belong to:

  • Kingdom → Animalia.
  • Phylum → Chordata.
  • Class → Mammalia.
  • Order → Primates.
  • Family → Hominidae.
  • Genus → Homo.
  • Species → Homo sapiens.
111. Primates
  • Primates generally have forward-facing eyes.
  • Many possess grasping hands.
  • Opposable digits are common.
  • Primates have relatively large brains for body size.
  • Humans are members of the ape lineage.
112. Hominidae
  • Hominidae is the great-ape family.
  • It includes humans, chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans.
  • Humans are not outside the ape evolutionary group.
113. Bipedalism
  • Habitual upright walking on two legs is a major feature of hominin evolution.
  • Bipedal adaptations appeared before the large brain size characteristic of later Homo.
  • Pelvis, spine and lower limbs show adaptations for bipedal locomotion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Early Hominin Trend → Bipedalism Before Major Brain Expansion

114. Australopithecus
  • Australopithecus species lived in Africa.
  • They were habitual bipeds.
  • They had smaller brains than later Homo.
  • Australopithecus afarensis is associated with the famous fossil “Lucy.”
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lucy → Australopithecus afarensis

115. Lucy
  • Lucy is a partial skeleton discovered in Ethiopia in 1974.
  • It belongs to Australopithecus afarensis.
  • It lived about 3.2 million years ago.
  • The fossil provided important evidence for early bipedalism.
116. Genus Homo
  • Genus Homo includes modern humans and several extinct relatives.
  • Members generally show increasing dependence on tools and complex behaviour compared with earlier hominins.
  • Brain size generally increased across some Homo lineages, though evolution was not strictly linear.
117. Homo habilis
  • Homo habilis means handy man.
  • It lived in Africa.
  • It is associated with early stone-tool traditions.
  • It had a larger brain than australopithecines on average.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homo habilis → Early Stone Tools

118. Homo erectus
  • Homo erectus had a body form well adapted for long-distance walking.
  • It spread beyond Africa.
  • It is associated with more advanced stone tools.
  • Controlled use of fire is often associated with Homo erectus populations, though archaeological evidence varies by site and date.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homo erectus → Early Widespread Dispersal Out of Africa

119. Neanderthals
  • Neanderthals are classified as Homo neanderthalensis in common modern treatment.
  • They lived in Europe and western Asia.
  • They were adapted to cold environments.
  • Genetic evidence shows interbreeding between Neanderthals and ancestors of many modern non-African humans.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Neanderthals were not simply direct “primitive stages” leading linearly to modern humans.

120. Homo sapiens
  • Homo sapiens originated in Africa.
  • Fossil and genetic evidence places the emergence of anatomically modern humans hundreds of thousands of years ago.
  • Modern humans later dispersed across the world.
  • Homo sapiens is the only surviving human species today.
121. Out-of-Africa Model
  • Modern humans evolved primarily in Africa.
  • Populations later dispersed from Africa.
  • They interbred to some extent with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
  • Modern human ancestry therefore includes limited contributions from archaic human populations.
122. Denisovans
  • Denisovans are an extinct archaic human group identified largely through DNA evidence.
  • They are closely related to Neanderthals.
  • Genetic traces remain in some modern populations, especially in parts of Asia and Oceania.
123. Human Evolution — Important Sequence for Exams

A simplified traditional sequence often used in basic exams is:

Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Archaic Homo forms → Homo sapiens

⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Actual human evolution was branching and overlapping, not a single straight sequence.

124. Brain Size and Human Evolution
  • Brain size increased substantially in some later Homo lineages.
  • Human evolution also involved changes in cognition, language, social behaviour and culture.
  • Brain size alone does not determine intelligence.
125. Tools and Human Evolution
  • Stone-tool technologies provide evidence of behavioural evolution.
  • Oldowan tools are associated with early Homo and perhaps some earlier hominins.
  • Acheulean hand axes are strongly associated with Homo erectus and related populations.
126. Cultural Evolution
  • Humans transmit information culturally as well as genetically.
  • Language, technology and social learning allow rapid behavioural change.
  • Cultural evolution can occur much faster than genetic evolution.
127. Coevolution
  • Coevolution occurs when two interacting species exert reciprocal evolutionary pressures on each other.
  • Flowering plants and pollinators provide examples.
  • Hosts and parasites can also coevolve.
128. Sexual Selection
  • Sexual selection favours traits that increase mating success.
  • It can operate through mate choice.
  • It can also operate through competition for mates.
  • Peacock tails are a classic example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sexual Selection → Reproductive/Mating Advantage

129. Charles Darwin and Sexual Selection
  • Darwin extensively discussed sexual selection in The Descent of Man.
  • The book was published in 1871.
  • He distinguished sexual selection from natural selection.
130. Kin Selection
  • Kin selection can favour behaviours that help genetic relatives.
  • It is related to inclusive fitness.
  • Alarm calls and cooperative behaviour can sometimes be analysed using kin-selection theory.
131. Co-adaptation
  • Co-adaptation refers to traits that work together effectively.
  • Natural selection may favour combinations of interacting traits.
  • Complex adaptations can evolve through accumulation of many beneficial changes.
132. Evolution Is Not Goal-Directed
  • Evolution has no predetermined final goal.
  • Natural selection acts on available variation under current conditions.
  • Organisms are not moving toward a universal “perfect” form.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Evolution ≠ Automatic progress from “lower” to “higher.”

133. Evolution and Complexity
  • Some lineages become more complex.
  • Others become simpler.
  • Parasites may lose structures that are unnecessary in their environment.
  • Evolution favours reproductive success, not maximum complexity.
134. Common Ancestry
  • Similarities among organisms can reflect descent from shared ancestors.
  • All known life shares fundamental biochemical features.
  • DNA, RNA, ATP and the genetic code are broadly universal.
135. Phylogeny
  • Phylogeny is the evolutionary history of a species or group.
  • Phylogenetic trees represent hypotheses of evolutionary relationships.
  • Branch points represent common ancestors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phylogeny → Evolutionary History

136. Cladistics
  • Cladistics groups organisms based on shared derived characteristics.
  • A clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants.
  • Molecular evidence is widely used in modern cladistics.
137. Clade
  • A clade is a monophyletic group.
  • It contains a common ancestor and all descendants of that ancestor.
  • Modern classifications aim increasingly to reflect clades.
138. Homology in DNA
  • Homologous genes share evolutionary origin.
  • DNA sequence similarity can reveal relationships not obvious from external appearance.
  • Molecular homology is a major tool in evolutionary biology.
139. Molecular Clock
  • A molecular clock uses accumulation of genetic changes to estimate divergence times.
  • Mutation rates vary among genes and lineages.
  • Fossil calibration is often required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Molecular Clock → DNA Change + Divergence Time

140. Evolution of Resistance — Direct Evidence

Observed evolutionary changes include:

  • Antibiotic resistance.
  • Insecticide resistance.
  • Herbicide resistance.
  • Changes in pathogen populations.
  • Changes in beak size in wild bird populations.
  • Evolution is therefore directly observable over short timescales.
141. Evolution and Environment
  • Environmental change alters selection pressures.
  • A trait beneficial today may become neutral or harmful later.
  • Evolutionary fitness is environment-dependent.
142. Extinction and Evolution
  • Extinction removes lineages.
  • It also opens ecological opportunities for surviving groups.
  • Mammal diversification accelerated after the end-Cretaceous extinction.
143. Evolution of Birds
  • Modern birds evolved from feathered theropod dinosaurs.
  • Fossils document numerous transitional dinosaur-bird features.
  • Archaeopteryx is historically famous but is not the only transitional fossil known.
144. Evolution of Whales
  • Whales evolved from terrestrial mammalian ancestors.
  • Fossils document stages from land-adapted mammals to fully aquatic whales.
  • Whale forelimbs are homologous with other mammalian forelimbs.
145. Evolution of Horses
  • Horse evolution is documented by a rich fossil record.
  • Changes included body size, teeth and limb structure.
  • Horse evolution was branching rather than a perfectly straight line.
146. Vestigial Pelvis in Whales
  • Modern whales retain reduced pelvic bones.
  • These structures are remnants of hind-limb-supporting structures in terrestrial ancestors.
  • They provide evidence for evolutionary history.
147. Atavism
  • Atavism is rare reappearance of an ancestral characteristic.
  • It can occur when developmental pathways retained in the genome are unusually expressed.
  • Examples occasionally cited include tail-like structures in humans.
148. Evolutionary Developmental Biology
  • Evolutionary developmental biology is often called evo-devo.
  • It studies how changes in developmental genes produce evolutionary changes.
  • Hox genes are important regulators of body-pattern development.
149. Hox Genes
  • Hox genes help determine body-region identity during development.
  • Related Hox genes occur across many animal groups.
  • Their conservation supports deep common ancestry.
150. Fossil Living Forms — “Living Fossil” Term
  • “Living fossil” is an informal term for living organisms that retain many ancient-looking characteristics.
  • It does not mean the species has stopped evolving.
  • Examples traditionally cited include Limulus, coelacanth and Ginkgo.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Living fossil ≠ Evolutionarily unchanged.

151. Limulus
  • Limulus is the horseshoe crab.
  • It is an arthropod, not a true crab in the crustacean sense.
  • It is traditionally called a living fossil.
152. Coelacanth
  • Coelacanths are ancient lineages of lobe-finned fishes.
  • Living coelacanths were scientifically rediscovered in 1938.
  • They are traditionally described as living fossils.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coelacanth Rediscovery → 1938

153. Ginkgo
  • Ginkgo biloba is an ancient seed-plant lineage.
  • It is the only living species of its major group.
  • It is commonly called a living fossil.
154. Important Evolution Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • Lamarck → Acquired characters.
  • Weismann → Germ-plasm concept.
  • Darwin → Natural selection.
  • Wallace → Independent natural-selection theory.
  • Herbert Spencer → Survival of the fittest.
  • Hugo de Vries → Mutation theory.
  • Oparin → Chemical evolution.
  • Haldane → Chemical evolution.
  • Miller and Urey → Prebiotic organic molecules.
  • Gould and Eldredge → Punctuated equilibrium.
155. Important Dates
  • Lamarck's Philosophie Zoologique → 1809.
  • Darwin's HMS Beagle voyage → 1831–1836.
  • Darwin-Wallace presentation → 1858.
  • Origin of Species → 1859.
  • Descent of Man → 1871.
  • Miller-Urey experiment → 1953.
  • Punctuated equilibrium proposal → 1972.
156. Must-Memorise Evolution Evidence
  • Fossils → Historical evidence.
  • Homologous organs → Common ancestry/divergent evolution.
  • Analogous organs → Convergent evolution.
  • Vestigial structures → Ancestral remnants.
  • Embryology → Developmental similarities.
  • Biogeography → Geographic patterns.
  • DNA/protein similarity → Molecular evidence.
157. Must-Memorise Mechanisms
  • Mutation → New alleles.
  • Recombination → New allele combinations.
  • Natural selection → Differential reproductive success.
  • Genetic drift → Random frequency change.
  • Gene flow → Allele movement.
  • Sexual selection → Mating advantage.
158. Must-Memorise Speciation Links
  • Allopatric → Geographic separation.
  • Sympatric → Same geographic region.
  • Prezygotic barrier → Before fertilisation.
  • Postzygotic barrier → After fertilisation.
  • Polyploidy → Important plant speciation mechanism.
159. TNPSC Traps
  • Evolution occurs in populations across generations.
  • Individuals do not evolve because they need to.
  • Origin of life and evolution are different questions.
  • Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation under ordinary conditions.
  • Oparin and Haldane proposed chemical evolution.
  • Miller-Urey experiment produced organic molecules, not life.
  • Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired characters.
  • Darwin and Wallace are associated with natural selection.
  • Origin of Species was published in 1859.
  • Herbert Spencer coined survival of the fittest.
  • Fitness means reproductive success.
  • Natural selection is not random, though mutations generating variation are not directed toward need.
  • Mutation creates new alleles.
  • Genetic drift is strongest in small populations.
  • Founder effect and bottleneck are forms of drift.
  • Gene flow moves alleles between populations.
  • Antibiotic resistance is evolution by natural selection.
  • DDT/pesticide resistance is also natural selection.
  • Homologous organs → Same origin, different functions.
  • Analogous organs → Different origin, similar functions.
  • Homologous → Divergent evolution.
  • Analogous → Convergent evolution.
  • Vestigial does not mean absolutely useless.
  • Archaeopteryx is a transitional fossil.
  • Peripatus is a traditional connecting-link example.
  • Fossils occur mainly in sedimentary rocks.
  • Carbon-14 is unsuitable for extremely ancient geological rocks.
  • Speciation requires genetic divergence and reproductive isolation.
  • Allopatric speciation involves geographic isolation.
  • Polyploidy is important in plant speciation.
  • Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium represents a non-evolving ideal population.
  • Humans did not evolve from modern chimpanzees.
  • Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor.
  • Human evolution was branching, not a straight ladder.
  • Lucy is Australopithecus afarensis.
  • Homo habilis is associated with early stone tools.
  • Homo erectus dispersed beyond Africa.
  • Neanderthals interbred with ancestors of many modern humans.
  • Birds evolved from theropod dinosaurs.
  • “Living fossils” continue to evolve.
160. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Evolution → Population change.
  • Pasteur → Biogenesis.
  • Oparin-Haldane → Chemical evolution.
  • Miller-Urey → 1953.
  • Lamarck → Acquired characters.
  • Weismann → Germ plasm.
  • Darwin → Natural selection.
  • Wallace → Natural selection.
  • Origin of Species → 1859.
  • Spencer → Survival of fittest.
  • Mutation → New allele.
  • Drift → Random.
  • Gene flow → Migration.
  • Founder → Drift.
  • Bottleneck → Drift.
  • Homologous → Same origin.
  • Analogous → Same function.
  • Homologous → Divergent.
  • Analogous → Convergent.
  • Archaeopteryx → Transitional fossil.
  • Peripatus → Connecting-link example.
  • Speciation → New species.
  • Allopatric → Geography.
  • Sympatric → Same area.
  • Polyploidy → Plant speciation.
  • Hardy-Weinberg → Equilibrium.
  • Lucy → Australopithecus afarensis.
  • H. habilis → Tools.
  • H. erectus → Dispersal.
  • H. sapiens → Modern human.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is evolution? → Heritable change in populations across generations.
  • Does an individual organism evolve during its lifetime? → No, evolution is population-level across generations.
  • Origin of life and evolution same? → No.
  • Approximate age of Earth? → 4.54 billion years.
  • Old theory of life arising from non-living matter under ordinary conditions? → Spontaneous generation.
  • Scientist who used meat-and-maggot experiments? → Francesco Redi.
  • Scientist associated with swan-neck flask experiment? → Louis Pasteur.
  • Pasteur's experiment supported? → Biogenesis.
  • Biogenesis means? → Life arises from pre-existing life.
  • Who proposed chemical evolution? → Oparin and Haldane.
  • Experiment producing amino acids under simulated early-Earth conditions? → Miller-Urey experiment.
  • Year? → 1953.
  • Did Miller-Urey create life? → No.
  • Hypothesis proposing early RNA as genetic and catalytic molecule? → RNA world hypothesis.
  • Catalytic RNA called? → Ribozyme.
  • Major early oxygen-producing organisms? → Cyanobacteria.
  • Evolutionary theory of acquired characters? → Lamarckism.
  • Lamarck's major evolutionary book year? → 1809.
  • Lamarck's famous mechanism? → Use and disuse plus inheritance of acquired characters.
  • Scientist associated with germ-plasm theory? → August Weismann.
  • Scientist most associated with natural selection? → Charles Darwin.
  • Darwin's ship? → HMS Beagle.
  • Beagle voyage? → 1831–1836.
  • Island group important to Darwin? → Galápagos Islands.
  • Darwin's finches illustrate? → Adaptive radiation.
  • Scientist who independently proposed natural selection? → Alfred Russel Wallace.
  • Darwin-Wallace joint presentation year? → 1858.
  • Origin of Species published? → 1859.
  • Natural selection requires? → Heritable variation plus differential reproductive success.
  • Who coined “survival of the fittest”? → Herbert Spencer.
  • Meaning of fitness in evolution? → Reproductive success.
  • Does natural selection act because organisms “need” a trait? → No.
  • Main source of new alleles? → Mutation.
  • Scientist associated with mutation theory? → Hugo de Vries.
  • Recombination occurs through? → Crossing over, independent assortment and fertilisation.
  • Movement of alleles between populations? → Gene flow.
  • Random change in allele frequencies? → Genetic drift.
  • Genetic drift strongest in? → Small populations.
  • New population started by few individuals causes? → Founder effect.
  • Sharp reduction in population causes? → Bottleneck effect.
  • Directional selection favours? → One extreme phenotype.
  • Stabilising selection favours? → Intermediate phenotype.
  • Disruptive selection favours? → Both extremes.
  • Human-directed breeding called? → Artificial selection.
  • Antibiotic resistance illustrates? → Natural selection.
  • Industrial melanism classic organism? → Peppered moth.
  • Scientific name of peppered moth? → Biston betularia.
  • Evidence for evolution includes? → Fossils, anatomy, embryology, biogeography and molecular data.
  • Study of fossils? → Palaeontology.
  • Fossils occur mainly in? → Sedimentary rocks.
  • Important dinosaur-bird transitional fossil? → Archaeopteryx.
  • Archaeopteryx possessed bird feature? → Feathers/wings.
  • Reptile/dinosaur-like features? → Teeth, clawed fingers and long bony tail.
  • Traditional connecting link between annelids and arthropods? → Peripatus.
  • Homologous organs have? → Same basic origin but different functions.
  • Example of homologous organs? → Human arm, whale flipper and bat forelimb.
  • Homologous organs indicate? → Divergent evolution/common ancestry.
  • Analogous organs have? → Similar function but different evolutionary origin.
  • Analogous organs indicate? → Convergent evolution.
  • Example? → Bird wing and insect wing.
  • Vestigial organ means? → Reduced ancestral structure.
  • Does vestigial mean completely useless? → No.
  • Biogeography means? → Study of geographic distribution of organisms.
  • Wallace Line named after? → Alfred Russel Wallace.
  • Strong modern evidence of common ancestry? → DNA and protein sequence similarity.
  • Formation of new species? → Speciation.
  • Barrier preventing gene flow? → Reproductive isolation.
  • Allopatric speciation involves? → Geographic separation.
  • Sympatric speciation occurs? → Without geographic separation.
  • Important rapid plant speciation mechanism? → Polyploidy.
  • Adaptive radiation means? → One ancestral lineage diversifying into multiple ecological forms.
  • Classic adaptive-radiation example? → Darwin's finches.
  • Permanent disappearance of a species? → Extinction.
  • Largest major mass extinction? → End-Permian extinction.
  • Non-avian dinosaurs disappeared around? → 66 million years ago.
  • Major cause of end-Cretaceous extinction? → Chicxulub asteroid impact.
  • Hardy-Weinberg principle describes? → Genetic equilibrium in an ideal population.
  • Hardy-Weinberg equation? → p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
  • Hardy-Weinberg conditions include? → Large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration and no selection.
  • Microevolution means? → Allele-frequency changes within populations.
  • Macroevolution includes? → Speciation and large-scale evolutionary patterns.
  • Punctuated equilibrium proposed by? → Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge.
  • Year? → 1972.
  • Scientific name of modern humans? → Homo sapiens.
  • Human order? → Primates.
  • Human family? → Hominidae.
  • Did humans evolve from modern chimpanzees? → No.
  • Human-chimp relationship? → Share a common ancestor.
  • Major early hominin adaptation before large brains? → Bipedalism.
  • Lucy belongs to? → Australopithecus afarensis.
  • Lucy discovered where? → Ethiopia.
  • Lucy discovery year? → 1974.
  • Approximate age of Lucy? → 3.2 million years.
  • Homo habilis means? → Handy man.
  • Homo habilis associated with? → Early stone tools.
  • Homo erectus important for? → Early widespread dispersal beyond Africa.
  • Neanderthal scientific name commonly? → Homo neanderthalensis.
  • Did Neanderthals interbreed with modern-human ancestors? → Yes.
  • Modern humans originated primarily in? → Africa.
  • Evolution of humans was straight ladder or branching? → Branching.
  • Birds evolved from? → Theropod dinosaurs.
  • Whales evolved from? → Terrestrial mammalian ancestors.
  • “Living fossil” means no evolution? → No.
  • Traditional living-fossil example? → Coelacanth.
  • Coelacanth rediscovered? → 1938.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Lamarck → acquired characters; Darwin + Wallace → natural selection; Miller-Urey → 1953; Homologous → divergent; Analogous → convergent; Allopatric → geographic isolation; Hardy-Weinberg → genetic equilibrium.
